judge_input.description:
### Description

What this PR does is go ahead and implement both `mockThrow(foo)` and also `mockThrowOnce(foo)`, and it does so specifically as convenient shorthands, the first one standing in for `mockImplementation(() => { throw foo })` and the second one standing in for `mockImplementationOnce(() => { throw foo })` respectively.

The reasoning here is that having a non-error path together with an error path for the synchronous functions (that is to say, `mockReturnValue` taken together with `mockThrow`) is something that ends up nicely mirroring the asynchronous counterparts of them (namely, `mockResolvedValue` taken together with `mockRejectedValue`), and, beyond just that, it also goes on to make the synchronous error paths immediately and clearly visible, as well as intention-revealing, right there within the tests themselves.

I am, for what it is worth, entirely open to renaming these two if that is something that happens to be wanted, though. I did go and consider the name `mockThrownValue` at one point, but in the end I just didn't really end up seeing the need for going with it.

> [!NOTE]
> `pnpm run test` → All pass  
> `pnpm run test:ci` → Fails due to an existing test that happens to be skipped only in the case when `GITHUB_ACTIONS` is set
>
> Affected test: `test/cli/test/watch/stdin.test.ts:93`  
> As far as I am aware of it, it is entirely and completely unrelated to any of the changes that were actually made here in this particular PR of mine.

To restate the whole point of it once more for clarity: these two brand new helpers are there purely for the sake of convenience, giving you a short and readable way of writing out a mock that goes and throws, and they do this for both the case where you want it to throw every single time as well as the case where you only want it to throw just the one single time, and all of this is done without your ever having to go and write out the longer and more verbose `mockImplementation` form out by hand each and every single time that you happen to need it. In short, they are simply convenience shorthands, nothing more and nothing less than that, but ones that do end up making the resulting test code quite a bit shorter, much cleaner, and a good deal easier to read through at a glance for just about anyone who happens to come along to it later on down the line.

In that particular case where the feature in question happens to be a genuinely substantial one, or else in the case where it goes and introduces breaking changes of one kind or another without there having been any real discussion about it at all beforehand, then the PR its own self might very well end up simply being closed right out on you.
- [X] Ideally, the thing that you really ought to go and do here is to make sure to include a test of some sort, and specifically one that goes and fails without this PR of yours being in place, but which then goes on afterward to actually pass once it finally is properly in place.
- [X] Please, do not ever go and make any changes of any kind whatsoever at all to the `pnpm-lock.yaml` file, unless of course it happens to be the one particular case where you are, at that very same time, also going and introducing a brand new test example right along together with it as well.
- [X] Please do go right ahead and check the [Allow edits by maintainers](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/collaborating-with-pull-requests/working-with-forks/allowing-changes-to-a-pull-request-branch-created-from-a-fork) option there, doing so specifically and deliberately in order to help make the whole of the review process go along quite a bit faster than it otherwise ever would have done. Do please also take some careful note right here of the fact that this one particular option is not one that happens to be available at all whatsoever for any of those repositories that happen to be owned by Github organizations.

### Tests
- [X] Go right ahead and run the whole entire set of the tests, and do so specifically by way of making use of the `pnpm test:ci` command that is provided for exactly that purpose.

### Documentation

### Changesets
- [X] The changes that end up going over into the changelog are the particular ones that get themselves generated automatically, straight from the PR name its own self. Please, do go and make very sure indeed that it properly and clearly explains your changes, and does so in a manner that is genuinely understandable to whoever happens to be reading it, and please do also prefix each and every one of the changeset messages with one of either `feat:`, `fix:`, `perf:`, `docs:`, or else instead just `chore:`.

 ```
 
+## mockThrow <Version>4.1.0</Version> {#mockthrow}
+
+```ts
+function mockThrow(value: unknown): Mock<T>
+```
+
+Accepts a value that will be thrown whenever the mock function is called.
+
+```ts
+const myMockFn = vi.fn()
+myMockFn.mockThrow(new Error('error message'))
+myMockFn() // throws Error<'error message'>
+```
+
+## mockThrowOnce <Version>4.1.0</Version> {#mockthrowonce}
+
+```ts
+function mockThrowOnce(value: unknown): Mock<T>
+```
+
+Accepts a value that will be thrown during the next function call. If chained, every consecutive call will throw the specified value.
+
+```ts
+const myMockFn = vi
+  .fn()
+  .mockReturnValue('default')
+  .mockThrowOnce(new Error('first call error'))
+  .mockThrowOnce('second call error')
+
+expect(() => myMockFn()).toThrow('first call error')
+expect(() => myMockFn()).toThrow('second call error')
+expect(myMockFn()).toEqual('default')
+```
+
